Descriptors associated with the primary active site, including electronegativity, H adsorption energy, and OH adsorption energy, dominate the prediction, whereas work function and M–M bond energy reflect secondary electronic-structure and local-environment effects.
In addition, the importance of M–M bond energy and work function suggests that H/D separation is subject to secondary tuning by electronic structure and the local environment. The work function,

as a proxy for interfacial electron availability, can influence the coupling between electron transfer and O–H/O–D bond cleavage in the Volmer transition state. Meanwhile, M–M bond energy reflects framework rigidity/strain and d-band modulation, thereby affecting the vibrational frequencies of H*/D* and the curvature of the reaction barrier.

Overall, H/D separation arises from isotope-dependent differences in the adsorption–reaction potential-energy surface at the active site, with electronegativity and H/OH adsorption energetics describing the local environment that controls water dissociation and H*/D* evolution.
The bimetallic architecture further tunes this landscape through work-function shifts and M–M bonding, ultimately modulating the extent of isotopic separation.
All these binding strength and bond energies correlate with the zero-point energies of the H
M bonds in the Volmer step.

In summary, we present an integrated

platform that advances electrocatalytic H/D separation as a practical complement to green hydrogen production. By coupling end-to-end automation—catalyst synthesis, electrochemical evaluation, and online isotope quantification—with real-time data acquisition and analysis, the system enables rapid, reproducible discovery of catalysts that simultaneously target isotope selectivity and hydrogen-evolution performance.

From the collected large-scale dataset, interpretable machine learning resolves a compact descriptor map in which electronegativity and H/OH adsorption energetics govern H/D separation, with LSV-derived activity, work function, and M–M bonding acting as secondary descriptors.

Guided by this map, multi-objective Bayesian optimization autonomously expands the activity–selectivity Pareto front, and its sampling trajectory follows the same physically meaningful descriptor trends, indicating feedback-driven, interpretable convergence rather than unconstrained black-box search.
Long-term galvanostatic operation further confirms that selected catalysts retain both separation performance and activity. More broadly, this work demonstrates a general strategy for data-centric,
autonomous catalyst discovery that can accelerate the development of electrochemical technologies critical to a low-carbon energy future.
